intro.title: Hello, I'm Ming
intro.desc: I am currently pursuing a Master's degree in Applied Data Science at the University of Victoria. My work and research interests focus on data science, machine learning, and microbial statistics. My projects related to large-scale data analysis and applied statistical modeling.

recent.title: 🧭 Highlights of the Year
recent.intro:
Over the past year, I have developed practical skills in machine learning, natural language processing, and large-scale data modelling and analysis.

My projects cover several areas of applied data science. I developed statistical simulations in Python and R to compare imputation methods for sparse microbiome data. I built a cost-aware AI agent routing model using XGBoost and off-policy evaluation, maintaining about 93% of the best agent’s merge rate at 71% of the cost. I also developed a fake-news classification pipeline using TF-IDF and Linear SVM, achieving 95.56% accuracy, and completed a local Gradio application for article prediction.

Other projects include implementing PCA from scratch for sentiment classification and building a PySpark ETL pipeline that transformed MovieLens data for Neo4j knowledge graphs and Power BI dashboards. These experiences have strengthened my ability to work with Python, R, SQL, PySpark, machine learning models, statistical evaluation, and end-to-end data pipelines.

project1.title: A Novel Statistical Method for Handling Zeros in Microbiome Data
project1.desc:
In this study, I designed and implemented simulation experiments for biological data to systematically evaluate and compare four widely used imputation methods. The evaluation was conducted using a range of statistical and machine learning metrics, including reconstruction error and ecological diversity preservation, to assess the performance of each method under complex biological data settings.

The entire research workflow was built as an end-to-end analysis pipeline using Python and R, incorporating compositional data analysis and phylogenetic distance matrix computation. In addition, I incorporated multiple complex parameters into the biostatistical simulation models to examine their simulation fidelity and computational efficiency, as well as to explore strategies for improving model runtime performance.

project2.title: Cost-Aware AgentRouter: A Cheaper Coding-Agent Frontier
project2.desc:
This project examined whether routing coding tasks across multiple AI agents, including Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Devin, and Claude Code, could reduce cost while maintaining the pull request merge rate.

A balanced sample of 25,580 pull requests was created from the full AIDev dataset of about 932,000 pull requests, with 5,116 samples for each agent. An XGBoost regression model was trained using task features and agent identity. Routing policies were evaluated using the direct method, inverse propensity scoring, doubly robust estimation, and bootstrap testing.

The results showed that the best agent could not be clearly identified based only on merge success. A simple estimate ranked Codex first, while the adjusted estimate favored the learned routing model. However, the difference remained within the range of estimation uncertainty because agent assignments were strongly affected by selection bias.

The clearest improvement came from cost reduction. Under the selected cost assumptions, only Codex and Copilot were cost-efficient. The routing model assigned suitable tasks to the cheaper Copilot while keeping more difficult tasks with Codex. It maintained about 93 percent of the best agent’s merge rate at only 71 percent of the cost. The result remained significant under paired and two-level bootstrap tests.

project3.title: Identifying Fake News Through Text Mining and Model Comparison
project3.desc:
This team project built a machine learning pipeline to classify articles in the WELFake dataset as real or fake using only the title and article text. The original dataset contained 72,134 articles and was reduced to 62,590 complete, deduplicated records after cleaning. Author and source information were not used.

I am responsible for the core work in this project. I trained Linear SVM, Decision Tree, and Random Forest models using the team’s shared TF-IDF features. I also created confusion matrices, reviewed false-positive and false-negative cases, and compared each model with the Logistic Regression baseline.

Using combined title and body text with TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams, Linear SVM gave the best result, reaching 95.56% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.9498. Random Forest achieved 93.47% accuracy, while Decision Tree reached 88.70%. Linear SVM and Logistic Regression misclassified 235 of the same articles, suggesting that the two linear models struggled with similar difficult cases.

The full pipeline and a local Gradio prediction app have been completed. The final report is still being prepared, so the project repository currently contains the most complete results.

project4.title: Predicting Market Trends Through Sentiment Analysis of Product Reviews
project4.desc:
This project built a complete sentiment classification pipeline using the UCI Sentiment Labelled Sentences dataset. The dataset contains 3,000 reviews from Amazon, IMDB, and Yelp, with an equal number from each source. After cleaning, the text was converted into 2,097 TF-IDF features. A linear SVM was tuned using 5-fold stratified cross-validation and achieved an average validation accuracy of 80.46% at (C = 0.5).

The main goal was to test whether PCA could improve the model by reducing the number of features. PCA was implemented in NumPy and checked against the scikit-learn version. Without PCA, the TF-IDF and SVM model achieved 79.00% test accuracy. Reducing the data to 450 dimensions lowered accuracy to 73.33%, while 600 dimensions resulted in 72.67%.

The results showed that PCA was not suitable for this task. Important sentiment information was spread across many words rather than a small number of main components. As a result, reducing the dimensions removed useful information. PCA also converted the sparse TF-IDF matrix into a dense matrix, which increased training time without improving accuracy.

project5.title: Cinematic Insights: Market Intelligence Driven by Movie Classification & Ratings
project5.desc:
This project developed a PySpark ETL pipeline for the MovieLens Latest Small dataset, which includes about 100,000 ratings, 3,600 tags, 9,700 movies, and 600 users. The cleaned data was exported in two formats. Six CSV files were prepared for a Neo4j graph connecting users, movies, tags, and genres, while three summary tables were created for Power BI dashboards.

The pipeline cleaned data types, removed duplicates, extracted release years from movie titles, and split multiple genres into separate rows. It also removed low-quality records with no release year, genre, or user tags and manually corrected several known data issues before export.

Key statistics, including row counts, genre distribution, top-rated movies, active users, and common tags, were automatically saved to a text file so the results could be checked and reproduced.
